sources.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
sources.text: Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. sources.title: Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs
sources.text: The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

sources.title: Microsoft presenta un chip de IA que quiere reducir su dependencia de NVIDIA
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. Microsoft busca abaratar la inteligencia artificial y depender menos de NVIDIA y AMD para sus servicios de IA con Maia 300, que llegará a los centros de datos en 2027 con más memoria y eficiencia. Mientras la inteligencia artificial sigue expandiéndose por buscadores, asistentes, herramientas y plataformas de programación, las grandes tecnológicas se enfrentan a un nuevo reto: encontrar suficiente potencia de cálculo para sostener el crecimiento de sus modelos de IA . Y es que cada nueva generación de IA exige más recursos, más centros de datos, pero sobre todo, procesadores capaces de gestionar cantidades masivas de información . Esta situación ha convertido a NVIDIA en uno de los actores más importantes de la industria tecnológica . Sus chips se han transformado en la infraestructura sobre la que funcionan muchos de los sistemas de IA más avanzados del mercado, hasta el punto de que numerosas compañías dependen de ellos para desarrollar y desplegar sus servicios. Ahora Microsoft quiere reducir parte de esa dependencia con Maia 300 , su chip de inteligencia artificial de tercera generación. Según The Verge , este procesador se convertirá en una pieza central de la infraestructura que utilizará la compañía para impulsar sus servicios de IA durante los próximos años. El objetivo de Maia 300 no es llegar al mercado de consumo ni competir con procesadores para ordenadores domésticos, sino que está diseñado para los centros de datos de Microsoft y para ejecutar cargas de trabajo relacionadas con inteligencia artificial a gran escala. De hecho, la compañía prevé que comience a desplegarse en producción a partir de 2027 y que termine convirtiéndose en su principal sistema de inferencia de IA. Es decir, el proceso mediante el cual un modelo ya entrenado genera respuestas, redacta textos, crea imágenes, produce código o ejecuta acciones solicitadas por los usuarios. Según explicó Scott Guthrie, vicepresidente ejecutivo del grupo de nube de Microsoft, la empresa planea escalar la familia Maia hasta despliegues de varios gigavatios , situándola como una de las principales infraestructuras sobre las que funcionarán sus servicios de inteligencia artificial. Ese despliegue afecta directamente a plataformas como Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot , Microsoft Foundry y a los modelos desarrollados internamente por Microsoft. De hecho, Maia 200, la generación anterior, ya está ejecutando cargas de producción en estos servicios. Es importante mencionar que Microsoft asegura que Maia 300 ha sido diseñado para afrontar las necesidades de la siguiente generación de modelos de inteligencia artificial. Entre sus objetivos se encuentran los sistemas de razonamiento avanzado , las conversaciones que manejan grandes volúmenes de contexto y los agentes capaces de realizar tareas complejas compuestas por múltiples pasos consecutivos. Este tipo de sistemas requieren más capacidad de procesamiento y tiempos de respuesta cada vez más rápidos. La compañía afirma que Maia 300 puede ofrecer un 40% más de tokens por megavatio respecto a los principales sistemas basados en GPU . Esta métrica permite medir cuánta IA puede ejecutarse en relación con la energía consumida. Microsoft también sostiene que una configuración completa de 96 aceleradores alcanza hasta siete veces más rendimiento a escala de rack que Maia 200, lo que supone un importante salto respecto a la generación anterior. En lugar de integrar todas las funciones en una única pieza de silicio, Maia 300 divide tareas como la computación, el control de memoria y las funciones de entrada y salida en bloques especializados. Cabe mencionar que el procesador está construido utilizando el nodo N2P de TSMC , uno de los procesos de fabricación más avanzados disponibles actualmente para este tipo de hardware. En una industria cada vez más dependiente del hardware especializado, Microsoft quiere que una parte de Copilot y de sus futuros modelos funcione sobre tecnología diseñada por la propia compañía , ganando margen en un mercado donde NVIDIA ha reinado durante años.

sources.text: Introducing Microsoft-Decision-1, our new model for fast decision-making. It delivers top performance on structured decision tasks, outperforming both LLMs and other decision models in latency and quality. We’re already testing it across Microsoft for everything from incident response and quality control to scientific discovery. Available now in Foundry and soon through OpenRouter: https://lnkd.in/gNh5aW8b Satya, I read the full article, and congratulations to Achint Srivastava and the team. The line that stood out is about calibration. The article says applications use confidence to decide when to act, defer, or ask for review, so a 90% prediction should be right about nine times out of ten. The speed and the cost are strong: 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol, and $0.042 per million input tokens. That makes the threshold a leadership decision, not a technical setting. The use case of agent controls, where the model decides whether to continue, stop, retry, or hand off to a human, makes this concrete. Someone has to set where “act” ends and “ask for review” begins, own that line, and show the board what happened when the model was wrong.The question for every leader adopting a decision model: who owns the threshold? Once a model starts making structured decisions, the important question is not just accuracy. Teams also need clear thresholds, fallback rules, and visibility into why a decision was made, especially in workflows like incident response or quality control where a wrong call can propagate quickly. Congrats on the release, we benchmarked it on jevman, where AI decision models play Pac-Man. It landed in the top 10: https://opper.ai/jevman-benchmark / Satya , how do you share deep, technical industry expertise without making your posts too boring or dense for the average scroller? Interesting. Would love to see the different type of inputs support such as image, as this will unlock many possibilities. The interesting risk is in the name. A model trained to be good at structured decision tasks gets good at decisions that look like structured decision tasks. Evals reward the shape of a decision, not the consequences of one. In incident response that becomes an operational question, not a model question. A proposal the model makes and an action the model is allowed to take are not the same object. The difference is code, a log, and a human with context. The better the latency, the more tempting the merge. Whoever wraps this in provenance wins the enterprise contract. The model is half the product. Interesting... based on defence ISRC4 mission parameters , we built these into our prompt and governace design.. Missions and mission contexts, situations and assessments basically provides a " capsule' for strings of actions, understandings , decisions and intent... AI if its going into complex and intelligence based decision support, it probably needs these top level parameterised mission style containers.. Satya Nadella The calibration metrics are great, but in latency-critical scientific simulations, how does Microsoft-Decision-1 handle conflicting structured data. Does it force a fast decision, or output its uncertainty bounds? Exciting direction for AI, Satya ! 👏 As someone building production AI automation and agentic systems, I see huge potential in specialized decision models. Faster, more reliable decisions could significantly improve incident response and multi-agent workflows. Looking forward to exploring Microsoft-Decision-1 through OpenRouter! 🚀 Specialized decision models could make AI significantly more useful for real-world enterprise operations where speed and accuracy both matter. The key will be how reliably they translate strong benchmark results into better decisions across complex business workflows.

sources.title: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI
sources.text: Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand. Musk, Benioff, Huang, and now Nadella have all capitulated to Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ rebrand. When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as “ super intelligence ,” you’d be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the great AI rebrand he so desires. That Elon Musk was quick to jump on board , promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn’t surprising. When, hours after Donald Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Marc Benioff announced that Salesforce would rename AIForce to SIForce ; it seemed like a quick capitulation, but not entirely out of character. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attended the summit where the executive order requiring government agencies to use the term “super intelligence” was announced. He’s also aligned himself with Trump, saying he believes the danger posed by AI is overblown. So it was somewhat predictable that when Nvidia declared that it would “commit” $1 billion to scientific advancement, that included “ super intelligence research .” Of course, Huang has a lot to lose if he gets on Trump’s bad side. The latest to cave is Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, who attended the same AI summit as Huang along with Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jeff Bezos, Dario Amodei, and Musk. In a post calling for building an “ emergency brake ” for AI yesterday, Nadella repeatedly referred to the technology as “super intelligence.” During Trump’s second term, Silicon Valley has repeatedly tried to ingratiate itself with the administration, after having a much more contentious relationship during his first term.

sources.text: Silicon Valley’s AI partner ecosystem is changing as enterprises push artificial intelligence projects out of pilots and into production. In the region where much of the AI stack is invented, infrastructure providers are learning that selling to builders takes a different playbook. That shift is reshaping how Dell Technologies Inc. approaches its West Coast customers. Buyers in the region are among the most technically sophisticated anywhere and often prefer assembling their own stacks to buying packaged solutions, according to Sean O’Connor (pictured), regional manager of ENT West, large enterprise and acquisition, at Dell. “Silicon Valley is interesting because everybody here wants to build versus buy,” he said. “They’re very, very sharp and they’re very, very savvy when it comes to technology.” O’Connor spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at the Dell “ AI Leadership Symposium, ” during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell sells to Silicon Valley’s builders, its widening AI partner ecosystem and how quickly it can deploy AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.) Winning over those builders means demystifying consultative services rather than leading with them, O’Connor explained. Dell’s technology partnerships remain central to that effort, but the company’s definition of an ecosystem is widening. Proximity to Dell Technologies Capital, the company’s venture arm, gives Dell a line into the startups and developer communities its customers already talk to, he noted. “For us, that notion of ecosystem is starting to change,” he said. “Today we’re here with Intel [Corp.], we’re here with SHI [International Corp.], we’re here with Microsoft [Corp]. But that ecosystem also now is starting to bleed into private equity and venture capital.” Deployment speed is another priority for Dell’s AI partner ecosystem. Long-standing relationships with Nvidia Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc. give Dell’s field teams credibility in customer conversations, O’Connor explained. Dell also expanded its Dell AI Factory with Nvidia portfolio at its Dell Technologies World conference in May. “We’re rolling out 350 racks within two weeks,” he said. “There’s a lot of new partnerships that are coming up, and they’re coming up to speed very, very fast.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s “ AI Leadership Symposium “: (* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for Dell’s “AI Leadership Symposium.” Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.) stories.title: Share GPU clusters across teams with isolation and fairness using Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
stories.summary: A reference architecture for securely sharing one Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster across multiple teams, using AWS IAM Identity Center for authentication, per-team SageMaker Domains and Kubernetes namespaces for isolation, HyperPod Task Governance for fairness, and namespace-level cost allocation for chargeback.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Share GPU clusters across teams with isolation and fairness using Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
sources.text: Multiple teams within the same company increasingly need shared access to expensive GPU clusters for their generative AI operations, while maintaining isolation boundaries, resource fairness, and operational independence. Consider a data science team training large language models, a computer vision group running inference workloads, and a research team experimenting with new model architectures. All of them might need access to the same cluster. Without a well-designed multi-tenant (multi-team) architecture, organizations face uncontrolled resource consumption, weak isolation between teams, an inability to attribute shared GPU costs to the teams that incur them, and administrative overhead that slows down innovation. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built AI service that simplifies the management of large-scale compute clusters for gen AI workloads. It provides resilient, optimized clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or Slurm, so organizations can run distributed training, interactive development, and model inference at scale. At the same time, it automatically handles node health monitoring, fault recovery, and cluster lifecycle management. In this post, we present a reference architecture for building a multi-tenant environment on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with EKS. This architecture uses AWS IAM Identity Center for centralized authentication, per-team SageMaker AI domains for a tailored user experience, Kubernetes namespaces for workload isolation, HyperPod Task Governance for fair resource allocation, and namespace-level cost allocation for per-team spend visibility and chargeback. By the end of this post, you will have a clear blueprint for multiple teams to efficiently share a single HyperPod EKS cluster. The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of a multi-tenant HyperPod EKS deployment. In this example, two teams (Team A and Team B) share a single HyperPod EKS cluster, each operating within their own isolated namespace. Figure 1: High-level multi-tenant architecture for two teams sharing one HyperPod EKS cluster The architecture is structured as a layered flow from left to right, connecting user identity through authorization controls and into isolated workload namespaces on the cluster. On the far left, individual users from each team (User 1 from Team A, User 2 from Team B) interact with the system through two paths. Both paths authenticate through the AWS IAM Identity Center Portal, which federates with an external identity provider (such as Microsoft Entra ID) shown at the bottom-left. The first path is through CLI access. Users authenticate with aws sso login , which redirects them to the Identity Center portal, and then obtain temporary credentials from their team’s permission set to submit tasks directly to the EKS cluster with kubectl . In the diagram, the pink arrow flows from the CLI terminal across the top directly into the HyperPod EKS cluster. The second path is through the Identity Center portal directly, where users select the SageMaker Studio application to sign in to their team-specific SageMaker AI domain. Each team has a corresponding permission set (TeamA permission set, TeamB permission set) that carries the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies needed for CLI workflows. Identity Center automatically provisions an IAM role for each permission set, shown in the diagram as TeamA-permissionset-role and TeamB-permissionset-role (labeled “CLI/Console role”). This role serves as the IAM principal when users authenticate through aws sso login . From the Identity Center portal, users are routed to their team-specific SageMaker AI domain. Each domain (SageMaker AI domain Team A and SageMaker AI domain Team B) provides a dedicated Amazon SageMaker Studio GUI and is configured with a team-specific execution role ( TeamA-role and TeamB-role respectively). These domains serve as the primary workspace interface, so users can submit tasks from the GUI (shown by the pink arrows flowing toward EKS). At the EKS boundary, access entries map IAM roles to Kubernetes permissions. The diagram shows access entries for TeamA-role and TeamB-role (the Studio execution roles), which authorize requests originating from the SageMaker Studio GUI. Access entries must also be configured for the Identity Center-provisioned CLI/Console roles ( TeamA-permissionset-role and TeamB-permissionset-role ) to authorize requests arriving through kubectl . All access entries are associated with managed or custom role-based access control (RBAC) policies (represented by the key icon) and scoped to the team’s designated namespace. As a result, whether access originates from Studio or the CLI, users can only interact with resources in their own namespace. The cluster itself is depicted with two cross-cutting platform layers at the top: HyperPod Observability (for monitoring and dashboards) and HyperPod Task Governance (for compute quota management and scheduling priorities). Below these layers, the cluster is partitioned into Namespace A (Team A) and Namespace B (Team B). Within each namespace, teams can run their own HyperPod Spaces (interactive development environments), HyperPod PyTorch jobs (distributed training workloads), and HyperPod Inference endpoints (model serving). Beneath the cluster, the architecture includes two storage tiers. The first is a POSIX-compliant file system (Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon FSx for OpenZFS) organized into per-team shared directories ( /fsx/TeamA , /fsx/TeamB ) and per-user home directories ( /home/User1 , /home/User2 ). The second is per-team or shared Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets for object storage, governed by the team’s IAM execution role. This architecture isolates each team from authentication through authorization to workload execution, while sharing expensive GPU infrastructure efficiently. The foundation of any multi-tenant system is robust authentication: verif

sources.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
sources.text: Building a cluster scheduler to prioritize high-impact research while maintaining full occupancy On the AI Infrastructure team at Ai2, we’re responsible for providing the institute’s GPU compute capacity, specifically targeting large, distributed training workloads. We think about this task as a pyramid of four metrics that build on each other. The foundation is availability : how often the hardware is healthy and ready for work. Above this is occupancy : the fraction of available time assigned to a specific workload. Next is impact : how often the most valuable workloads are chosen to receive resources. The capstone of the pyramid is utilization : the fraction of GPU capacity used over the lifetime of a workload. This post is about improving the impact of our scheduling decisions. We recently replaced a priority-based scheduler with a system including GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract. As a result, we shifted the debate about how much GPU time each research project deserves from a case-by-case operational task to a transparent administrative budgeting process. At Ai2, we manage thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs arranged in clusters ranging in size from 88 to 1024 GPUs. These clusters are built for large-scale distributed training of AI models, and they serve a group of about 150 internal researchers whose work covers a diverse set of AI domains, including the full model flow of LLM and VLM training, robotics reinforcement learning (RL) simulation, and post-training for scientific agentic use cases. Like many labs, we have demand for GPU time that far exceeds supply. Based on submitted workloads, at any moment in time we have outstanding requests for 2-3x more GPUs than are available. One way to think about this is that every available GPU hour on our cluster has 2-3 different research workloads competing for it. Historically, we used a priority-based scheduler, and we allowed workloads to opt out of preemptability. Each team had a limit on concurrent GPUs that could be used by workloads which were protected from preemption. Preemptible workloads could exceed that limit on idle GPUs. This strategy produced predictable pathologies. For example, we observed instances of GPU “squatting” where users would park no-op workloads they could connect to when the need arose. This occurred because researchers found they could not launch debugging workloads with low enough latency to tackle problems in real time. We also observed priority inflation, where eventually 100% of scheduled workloads used HIGH priority. This meant that lower priority levels were starved of GPU time altogether. Since preemptability was optional, we also found that our on-call engineers spent a majority of their ticket response time negotiating the organized shutdown of non-preemptable workloads running on hosts with known maintenance problems. When these problems emerged, we were slow to identify their root causes. Our initial attempts to ensure the most important work received GPU time were focused on tighter control of how priorities were set, and, ultimately, working around the priority-based scheduler by explicitly assigning GPU monopolies to important projects. While we didn’t recognize it at first, we had built a perfect laboratory for observing the “tragedy of the commons.” Individuals were competing over a scarce, shared resource and, by seeking to maximize individual outcomes, achieving a non-optimal global result and abusing the underlying resource. We were far from the first to observe this kind of interaction. Resource allocation is a fascinating research domain that mixes algorithm development, economics, and system management. A central problem is that users often know the value of their own jobs better than the organization does, but they may have incentives to hide that value or hold on to resources even when doing so hurts total performance. For example, in their 2011 paper introducing Dominant Resource Fairness , Ghodsi et al. recount an anecdote in which a search company provided dedicated machines to jobs only if their users could guarantee high utilization. They soon discovered “users would sprinkle their code with infinite loops to artificially inflate utilization levels.” The hardware changes, but the fundamental problems that make resource allocation complex persist. The classic solution to a tragedy of the commons is to privatize the shared resource—owners are incentivized to maximize the value of their property. When we assigned teams monopolies over sets of GPUs, we were already doing a version of this, but it was too coarse. It caused GPUs to sit idle due to the seasonality of research. Teams are ready to run experiments and training at different times, so assigning a monopoly would ensure that there would be times when no jobs were ready to execute, with another team left waiting for capacity. We were manually solving a knapsack problem , trying to fit dynamically changing research needs into a static schedule. We wanted the ownership incentive, but we also wanted to maintain full occupancy of the GPUs. We decided to iterate on the ownership model. Instead of issuing teams GPUs, we chose to allocate a portion of GPU time. Predicting demand into the future would require knowing the result of novel science experiments, so it cannot be forecast with precision. Priority across research efforts, however, is a question of strategy, and it can be more easily debated and decided in advance. Instead of trying to solve the scheduling puzzle, we enabled leadership to think like investors. Before the workloads exist, decide how to fund each research effort with GPU time based on their judgment of its likely impact. The scheduler could then use that information when prioritizing arriving workloads. With this in mind, we devised a hierarchical system where managers could proportionally allocate GPU time to the projects and researchers they were respon

sources.title: Microsoft debuts multichiplet Maia 300 inference accelerator
sources.text: Microsoft Corp. today pulled back the curtains on Maia 300, its newest internally developed artificial intelligence accelerator. The chip is optimized for inference, the process of generating responses to AI queries. Microsoft estimates that it can process 40% more tokens per megawatt than “leading GPU-based systems,” which is likely a reference to Nvidia Corp. products. The company said the Maia chip series will become its primary source of inference capacity over time. Maia 300 features four computing chiplets made using Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s latest two-nanometer node. The chiplets are flanked by eight HBM4 modules with 288 gigabytes of combined capacity, the same amount as Nvidia Corp.’s flagship Rubin accelerator. However, Maia 300 has about 20% less memory bandwidth than Rubin. Memory bandwidth is a measure of how much fast data can be transferred to and from RAM. AI chips usually perform inference by repeatedly shifting data between their computing and memory circuits. That constant movement slows down processing. According to Microsoft, Maia 300 features a dataflow architecture designed to minimize data movement. When possible, the computing chiplets keep information in an internal SRAM cache instead of sending it to the HBM stacks. In situations where using HBM can’t be avoided, Maia 300’s computing chiplets send data to a memory stack that is physically nearby. That’s faster than transmitting information to an HBM stack on the other end of the chip. For added measure, Maia 300 compresses data into lightweight formats such as MXFP4. Those formats’ reduced size enables data to move faster inside the chip. “Narrower representations reduce memory footprint and data movement, allowing the system to support larger models, longer contexts, and more concurrent sessions within the same power envelope,” Microsoft executives Rani Borkar and Saurabh Dighe wrote in a blog post . Maia 300’s computing and memory modules are supported by what Microsoft calls a device control chiplet. It manages the flow of power to the processor’s core components, collects telemetry and performs other supporting tasks. There are also two other auxiliary chiplets that manage the movement of data in and out of the accelerator. Microsoft plans to deploy Maia 300 in trays that will feature four accelerators apiece. Those trays, in turn, will be placed in liquid-cooled racks with a total of 96 accelerators. Microsoft expects the racks to provide about seven times the token throughput of a system equipped with its previous-generation Maia 200 chip. The company debuted the latter accelerator in January and already uses it in production. Microsoft intends to group its Maia 300 racks into so-called superpods with a total of 12,288 accelerators. The individual chips will be linked together using a custom Ethernet-based network stack. The network can adjust how much bandwidth is allocated to in-rack traffic and how much is available for inter-rack communications, which enables it to tailor its configuration to each workload. The result is increased performance. Usually, chips exchange data differently depending on whether they’re in the same rack or in different racks. As a result, switching between the two networking modes requires them to use the host server’s central processing unit or a standalone network chip. Maia 300, in contrast, uses the “same communication semantics” for both tasks. That removes the need for the extra hardware and thereby makes clusters more efficient. “Jobs can use capacity across rack boundaries, reducing stranded accelerators when workload sizes do not align with the physical rack configuration,” Borkar and Dighe explained. Microsoft plans to start deploying Maia 300 in production next year. The company expects its custom silicon to power multiple gigabytes’ worth of AI computing capacity. sources.title: NVIDIA tiene motivos para preocuparse. Microsoft apuesta por su propio chip Maia 300 para su infraestructura de IA
sources.text: Cada vez que utilizamos una herramienta de inteligencia artificial, hay una infraestructura trabajando para ofrecernos una respuesta. Detrás de buena parte de esa capacidad de procesamiento encontramos los aceleradores de NVIDIA , una compañía que se ha convertido en uno de los grandes proveedores de la industria. Para empresas como Microsoft, que necesitan sostener servicios de IA a gran escala, depender de estos procesadores plantea una cuestión que va más allá de su rendimiento. También importa cuánto cuesta ampliar la infraestructura y hasta qué punto pueden controlar la tecnología que necesitan para seguir creciendo. La respuesta de Microsoft ya tiene nombre y calendario: Maia 300. L a compañía estadounidense ha presentado la tercera generación de sus aceleradores de inteligencia artificial y ha fijado para 2027 el comienzo de su despliegue en producción. La decisión va acompañada de un objetivo de mayor alcance: convertir Maia en su principal sistema de inferencia para productos y servicios de IA y ampliar sus despliegues a escala de varios gigavatios a partir de ese mismo año. Por ahora es una hoja de ruta anunciada, no una transformación concluida de sus centros de datos. Para entender el alcance de esta apuesta, conviene distinguir dos procesos que forman parte del funcionamiento de la inteligencia artificial. Una cosa es entrenar un modelo, utilizando grandes cantidades de datos para desarrollar sus capacidades, y otra es la inferencia, que comienza cuando alguien le hace una petición y espera una respuesta . Microsoft quiere reforzar especialmente esta segunda tarea con sus propios aceleradores. El proyecto no parte de cero: presentó Maia 100 en 2023 y Maia 200 , anunciado en enero de 2026, ya procesa cargas de trabajo reales, incluidas las de Microsoft Copilot. Esa experiencia está sirviendo para orientar el desarrollo de la siguiente generación. Maia 300 no está concebido simplemente como un procesador más potente, sino como un sistema en el que memoria, computación y comunicaciones trabajan de manera coordinada. Su arquitectura utiliza varios chiplets, componentes de silicio que reparten distintas funciones, y los destinados al cálculo se fabrican mediante el proceso N2P de TSMC. También incorpora ocho pilas de memoria HBM4, una tecnología que permite transferir grandes cantidades de datos a gran velocidad. Microsoft ha diseñado además un sistema de gestión del flujo de información mediante software para reducir movimientos innecesarios de datos y aprovechar mejor los recursos disponibles. Las cifras anunciadas apuntan a una mejora que Microsoft quiere medir no solo en rendimiento, sino también en consumo eléctrico. Según sus estimaciones, Maia 300 permitirá procesar un 40% más de tokens por megavatio que algunos de los principales sistemas basados en GPU, aunque no ha identificado los equipos utilizados como referencia. Los tokens son unidades en las que los modelos dividen el texto y otros contenidos para procesarlos. La compañía sostiene, además, que un rack con 96 aceleradores ofrecerá hasta siete veces el rendimiento en tokens por rack de Maia 200 , aunque también duplica el número de aceleradores. Son comparaciones diferentes, basadas en datos del fabricante y todavía sin una validación independiente publicada. Para llevar Maia 300 a esa escala hace falta algo más que fabricar chips. Microsoft también está preparando los sistemas completos que los alojarán: cada rack está diseñado para funcionar dentro de un límite de potencia de 167 kilovatios y permitir que más aceleradores trabajen de manera coordinada. Su hoja de ruta contempla comenzar en 2027 una expansión de la familia Maia hacia despliegues de varios gigavatios, sin fecha anunciada para alcanzar ese nivel. La escala importa porque la electricidad disponible y la capacidad física de las instalaciones condicionan cuánto pueden crecer estos servicios. Lo que estamos viendo va más allá de Microsoft. Google ya utiliza sus TPU y Amazon ofrece servidores basados en Trainium , dos ejemplos de grandes clientes de NVIDIA que también desarrollan soluciones propias . Esto no significa que hayan dejado de recurrir al fabricante estadounidense. De hecho, Amazon y NVIDIA anunciaron en agosto un plan para desplegar dos millones de GPU adicionales en AWS entre 2027 y 2028. Pero sí estamos ante un movimiento que merece atención: empresas que necesitan enormes cantidades de capacidad de procesamiento quieren disponer de tecnología propia para cubrir parte de esa demanda y reducir su dependencia de proveedores externos. En Xataka | La gran paradoja de la IA es que creará más empleo del que destruye. El problema es que casi nadie está preparado

stories.title: Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI
stories.summary: With GPT-5.6, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI
sources.text: With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads. Pollo AI ⁠ (opens in a new window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise. Even with generative AI, creators and marketers can struggle to navigate different tools and choose between models to get the result they want. Some may even abandon their projects in frustration. “We want to do for video what Canva did for design. We want to make it easy enough that more people can actually use it, not just the ones who already know how,” explains Bill Zhu, the founder and CEO of Pollo AI. Today, Pollo AI serves more than 26 million users who use the platform to create videos, ads, and visual content. The team’s first breakthrough was video templates. Now, 30% of creator sessions start from these templates or trending-format workflows. Building on this success, the company’s latest offering is Pollo Agent. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user. Pollo Agent interprets the user’s rough ideas and visual references, and then develops storylines, scene flows, and scripts. CTO Peter Zhou says OpenAI models stood out for their ability to understand ambiguous creative inputs and their multimodal capability, sharing: “GPT‑5.6 performed especially well there.” The team also said they value the OpenAI API’s stability and release cadence. To balance reasoning depth, speed, and cost, Pollo AI uses GPT‑5.6 for routing and GPT‑6 Astra for more challenging work, such as developing a narrative or planning scene revisions. This model mix lets the system match the level of reasoning to the task based on the user’s prompt. Pollo AI reports that users spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity. Pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals. Pollo AI’s primary users are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content quickly and easily too. Pollo’s Photo to Video Ads tool in its Marketing Studio suite uses OpenAI models to turn a still image and prompt into a short video. It’s designed to help small businesses and DTC brands generate product ads for social media in minutes rather than days. One Pollo AI user wanted to use a product photo to make a fragrance ad that felt luxurious. The static photo alone could not convey that mood, and a professional video shoot was beyond their budget. Using Photo to Video Ad, the user turned their starting image into a roughly 15-second video ad. The tool generated velvet textures, warm spotlights, and close-ups of the bottle to establish the mood across the sequence and ended it with the fragrance framed against deep red fabric. Another customer, a jewelry brand, wanted a bold editorial campaign image, but its budget could not stretch to a high-concept studio shoot. Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, the brand was able to turn its creative vision of its statement jewelry on a model seated beside a cheetah into reality. The tool framed the scene with dark drapery and warm lighting and ensured that the brand’s jewelry products were highly visible. The customer got a finished luxury campaign visual with lower production effort, time, and cost compared to live shoot. Pollo AI also makes it easy for customers to start with a product photo and leverage OpenAI models to turn it into an image that’s far more creative. For example, a beverage brand wanted its peach soda to feel playful and imaginative in an advertising campaign, but a standard studio product shot could not capture what the team had in mind. Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, which brings sharper details and faster generation to creative workflows, the team transformed a simple bottle image into a snowy miniature landscape, complete with a train, lizards, and sparkling droplets. The finished image created a playful scene the brand could use in its campaign. Pollo wants AI video to become part of everyday content creation over the next 12 months. For Zhu, that depends on making it even easier to turn an idea into an asset ready to post, test, or use in a campaign, something Pollo AI is enabled to deliver with the continued improvement of OpenAI models and image generation. “We think the AI shift in content creation will favor products that make creation more repeatable from the start, with stronger formats, less trial and error, and a simpler workflow around the models themselves,” he says.
